item.title: Tue AM · Planet Money: How bodegas led to the Yemeni coffeehouse explosion
item.itunes:title: Tue AM · Planet Money: How bodegas led to the Yemeni coffeehouse explosion
item.description:
There is a long-standing tradition of different immigrant groups arriving in the U.S. and specializing in one particular type of business. Think, nail salons run by people from Vietnam or Gujarati Indians owning motels and hotels.

Yemenis are another immigrant community that has largely clustered around one industry, in their case, bodegas and small grocery stores. There are thousands of these shops all over the country, despite Yemeni-Americans only making up around one-fortieth of one percent of the U.S. population, according to the last census. 

In the past 9 years, a new business success story has been built on top of that foundation: Yemeni coffee houses.

Today on the show, why some immigrant groups concentrate in a single industry, while others spread out to work in all sorts of jobs. And what it’s like for the next generation to try to expand on their parents’ success.

item.title: Mon AM · Planet Money: Are wildfires making the future uninsurable?
item.itunes:title: Mon AM · Planet Money: Are wildfires making the future uninsurable?
item.description:
Over the past decade, increasingly catastrophic wildfires have wrought unprecedented destruction and upended the basic math of the insurance industry. In some of the riskiest parts of the country, homeowners have seen spiking premiums or lost their coverage altogether.

Today on the show, we travel to the forested foothills of Northern California to see how communities in wildfire-prone areas are trying to conjure the private insurance market back into existence. What actually happens when a megafire comes knocking at your door. And what all this means for the biggest question: In the age of climate change, could the future simply become uninsurable?

item.title: Sun PM · Wildcard · Hit Parade: Clearly Canadian Edition
item.itunes:title: Sun PM · Wildcard · Hit Parade: Clearly Canadian Edition
item.description:
For decades, America’s Hot 100 pop chart has been regularly invaded by Canadian artists like Paul Anka, the Guess Who, Bryan Adams, Céline Dion, Justin Bieber, and Drake. Yet in Canada, some of these Canucks’ biggest hits aren’t considered fully “Canadian.”

Join Chris Molanphy for a look at how the country’s requirements for Canadian content, or CanCon, on radio, television, and other cultural outlets has influenced the music industry and entire careers on both sides of the border. From Kon Kan’s “I Beg Your Pardon” to Tate McRae’s recent “Housewife,” Chris explores how much credit, or blame, Canada’s radio rules deserve for what Americans hear on the pop charts.

For more chart history for the Great White North, check out Hit Parade’s recent episode on Celine Dion .

item.title: Sun PM · Philosophize This!: Episode #042 ... Optimism
item.itunes:title: Sun PM · Philosophize This!: Episode #042 ... Optimism
item.description:
On this episode, we explore the benefits and drawbacks of optimism. First, we examine the various motivations for pessimism, and hear what Winston Churchill, Ralph Waldo Emerson, and Marcus Aurelius have to say about optimism. Next, we think about the vastly different implications of optimism in our personal lives and optimism on a societal level. Finally, we find out why Voltaire thought it was preposterous to think that we’re living in the best of all possible worlds and why he said, "Optimism is the madness of insisting all is well when we are miserable." All this and more on the latest episode of Philosophize This!

item.itunes:title: Sat AM · Order of Man: Chicks Dig Scars | FRIDAY FIELD NOTES
item.description:
In this episode of Friday Field Notes, Ryan Michler breaks down the core fundamental needs that dictate relationship success or failure: women crave safety, while men crave respect. Drawing from his own 18-year marriage, divorce, and years of self-reflection, Ryan dispels common misconceptions around modern dating and red-pill rhetoric. He explains why safety isn't about avoiding conflict, but about consistent emotional regulation, clear leadership, and unwavering stability. Conversely, he addresses why men desperately need genuine respect and appreciation - not entitlement or passive compliance. Tune in to learn actionable ways both men and women can step up, fulfill each other's core needs, and build a resilient, long-lasting partnership.
